Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette: At sixty-six, Arthur still feels the ghost of that temperature on his skin whenever the thermostat shifts in a room. He was ten when his stepfather's hand closed around his forearm in the basement laundry room. The skin had been exactly fifty-eight degrees, a precise, chilling weight that pressed into the boy's flesh. That specific temperature on the skin is no longer just a detail; it is a tether. When a draft from an open window hits his wrist, a memory of the event comes to mind suddenly, and his own heart begins to race or pound without warning. He is certain that the coldness was a warning. He had come to believe that you never know what can happen next, so he watches for danger before his mind has even caught up to the moment. What frightened him most was not the strike itself, but the sudden, unannounced arrival of a threat that bypassed thought. Over the following years, this pattern settled into a daily rhythm. He avoids his own body by keeping his sleeves pulled down and refusing to check the pulse points on his wrists. In his current role as a software engineer, these habits take root in the open-plan tech floor. He notices potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment: a heavy letter opener on a receptionist's desk, a fire extinguisher mounted near the break room, the sharp edge of a monitor stand. When a colleague reaches out to tap his shoulder to ask a question about a deployment, his body reacts before he has even had time to think. His startle to touch fires first, jolting him upright. People can't be trusted. He avoids being touched by any form of physical contact with others, so he wears long-sleeved shirts in summer and turns slightly away when someone walks too close. Seeing people that he socialized with before the event now feels like stepping into a room he no longer belongs to. He is permanently an outsider now, watching teams huddle over whiteboards while he types in silence. Constant vigilance means he has to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, so he maps the exits of every conference room and notes the weight of the staplers on every desk. These adjustments accumulated over months and years, reshaping his days. He stopped going to the Friday afternoon beers with his former project leads, leaving them to wonder why he never answered the group chat. His wife began carrying the groceries to the trunk herself because she knew he would flinch if she tried to take a bag from his hands. The isolation was not chosen lightly; it was the only way to keep his nervous system from flooding. He had come to believe that people cannot be trusted to move gently or speak softly, so he kept his distance, protecting a quiet that felt safer than the noise of the world. At sixty-six, Arthur sat in a therapist's office and placed his hands flat on his knees, not to look at them, but to anchor them. He had finally come to seek help because the weight of watching for threats had grown too heavy to carry alone. He did not know if he wanted to forget the cold hand on his arm or simply learn to live beside it without flinching. He was most afraid of losing the careful control he had built, yet he was hoping, quietly, for a place where he could rest without checking the corners of the room.
